question: Does maximizing gradient norm along a loss-preserving symmetry orbit provide a theoretically justified and practically reproducible acceleration of gradient optimization, especially for multilayer neural networks?

key_findings.claim: The paper's distinctive contribution is to turn loss-preserving reparameterization into an active optimization subproblem: periodically choose an equivalent parameter point with a larger gradient norm, then resume the base optimizer.
key_findings.evidence: Algorithm 1 searches a symmetry orbit for g maximizing the squared gradient norm and replaces w by g·w without intending to change L. Earlier neural teleportation already preserved network function, explored loss level curves, and boosted gradients; this paper's genuine increment is the purposeful orbit search, its group-action constructions, and an attempted convergence account rather than random relocation.

key_findings.claim: Proposition 5.1 proves only an instantaneous continuous gradient-flow comparison under an exact differentiable invertible symmetry, not fewer discrete iterations, less wall-clock time, or end-to-end convergence acceleration.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 9 identifies dL/dt with minus the squared gradient norm in continuous flow, and Proposition 5.1 applies the chain rule through the action Jacobian. It does not control a finite learning rate, orbit-search error or cost, optimizer state, stability after the jump, or time to a target loss. The subsequent Hazan citation is also misstated: the smooth-GD result bounds a sum of squared gradient norms under its smoothness-limited step, whereas the paper prints an unsquared norm. Even the corrected aggregate upper bound does not imply that making one gradient larger requires fewer steps to convergence.

key_findings.claim: The finite-step result preserves a gradient-norm ordering only under a rapidly strengthening sufficient condition and does not compare losses or establish faster convergence.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 5.4 requires the initial gradient-norm ratio to exceed ((1+eta L)/(1-eta L))^T, obtained by combining worst-case Lipschitz upper and lower envelopes. Its conclusion is solely that the teleported trajectory's gradient norm remains at least as large after T steps. Different trajectories can have different directions and losses, so this ordering alone is not an optimization-rate theorem.

key_findings.claim: The one-teleportation optimality result is correct only for a specially engineered positive-definite quadratic with a transitive action that already depends on the known quadratic matrix.
key_findings.evidence: Sections 5.3 and C.3 construct g·w=A^(-1/2) rho(g) A^(1/2)w so that every ellipsoidal level set is intended to be a single O(n) orbit. The proof of Proposition C.1 silently replaces rho(g) by g and is therefore valid only for the standard representation, or more generally a sphere-transitive representation; it is false for an arbitrary representation such as the trivial one permitted by the statement. Under the required restriction, exact maximization selects an eigenvector associated with A's largest eigenvalue and gradient flow remains on that eigendirection. This existence example also assumes knowledge of A, exact matrix square roots, a transitive orbit, and exact orbit optimization; it does not justify the approximate GL updates used for networks. The optimizer is nonunique up to sign and any top-eigenspace multiplicity, despite Proposition C.2 calling it the solution.

key_findings.claim: The claimed equivalence to the Newton direction omits necessary regularity and sign conditions and is false as a same-direction statement for a negative Hessian eigenvalue.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma C.4 differentiates the gradient norm and invokes a Hessian, requiring more than the proposition's stated setup; the level set must also be regular enough that all tangent directions are orthogonal to a nonzero gradient, and H must be invertible before H^(-1) is used. Even if the gradient is a Hessian eigenvector, H^(-1)grad has the same orientation only for a positive eigenvalue; a negative eigenvalue reverses it. Standard Newton descent also uses -H^(-1)grad. The paper itself concedes that practical actions are nontransitive, the optimum can be unbounded, and exact every-step teleportation is not performed.

key_findings.claim: The exact neural-network symmetry is much narrower than the experimental setting: it requires bijective activations and a square full-rank hidden activation, while the experiments use rectangular sample-by-width matrices and a pseudoinverse that the paper admits is not a group action.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 4.3 derives a GL action using sigma^(-1) and h_(m-2)^(-1). Immediately afterward, the paper states that h_(m-2) must be square and full rank; when the number of examples n is below the hidden dimension, a left inverse may preserve the chosen output but fails the identity axiom. The regression uses four samples with hidden widths six and seven, and MNIST teleportation uses mini-batches of 20 with width 512, so neither realizes the proposition's exact group-action premise.

key_findings.claim: The released regression implementation does not preserve loss at teleportation, invalidating the central interpretation of its reported acceleration.
key_findings.evidence: The paper and code replace g by I+T and g^(-1) by I-T, although these are not inverses because (I-T)(I+T)=I-T^2, and they combine this approximation with a rectangular pseudoinverse. Section 6.1 writes the regression objective as the unscaled squared norm, while the released loss_multi_layer implements one half of that squared norm, changing the effective learning-rate and stopping-scale interpretation. Running the released three-layer regression at its paper-specified epoch-5 teleport across five seeds changed the code loss from 595.66 to 364.91, 685.54 to 90.59, 614.24 to 334.59, 576.01 to 347.27, and 575.07 to 51.85: direct reductions of 39-91%, not motion on a level set. Gradient-squared ratios were only 1.02-2.09. Thus Figure 3 can mix an immediate objective-changing update with later optimizer dynamics and cannot establish loss-invariant acceleration.

key_findings.claim: The Rosenbrock and Booth demonstrations are oracle-crafted proof-of-concept examples rather than evidence that useful symmetries can be discovered for an unknown objective.
key_findings.evidence: The construction first chooses an invertible mapping h that turns the target function into a Euclidean radius and then pulls SO(2) rotations back through h. For Rosenbrock and Booth, h is written from the known analytic formula and optimum. Figures 2 and 7 show favorable paths after this problem-specific construction, but the method supplies no procedure for learning h or discovering the action from a black-box objective.

key_findings.claim: The neural evidence is small, tuned, and incomplete: a toy regression supports only five-run curves, while MNIST shows faster training but earlier overfitting and slightly worse validation accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: The regression has three tiny matrices, four random examples, and teleportation hyperparameters selected by a grid search on the same problem. Figure 3 reports five-run uncertainty but no held-out task or statistical test. MNIST uses one shallow 512-512 MLP, one train/validation split, no test-set accuracy table, and no multi-seed error bars in Figures 4-5. The authors explicitly report limited validation benefit, detrimental AdaGrad validation loss, earlier overfit, and slightly worse validation accuracy.

anchors.section: Appendix D.2 tuning protocol and Figure 8

key_findings.claim: The runtime evidence does not establish robust wall-clock acceleration because teleportation has large constants, convergence is defined by a plateau criterion, and failed or diverged sweep points are omitted.
key_findings.evidence: A teleport costs O(d_max^2 n l t) plus layerwise pseudoinverses. Figure 6 shows polynomial scaling, and the text concedes that teleportation dominates runtime despite the same asymptotic order as an optimizer step. Figure 8 defines convergence as consecutive losses differing by less than 10^-3 on one unspecified CPU and omits settings that diverge or fail within 2,000 steps. Therefore 'most hyperparameter combinations' refers only to the surviving plotted settings, while a flat but suboptimal trajectory may also meet the stopping rule.

key_findings.claim: The public artifact is executable but is only a partial reproduction package and contains additional determinism and update-order defects.
key_findings.evidence: The first-party repository contains a README and four Python files for Rosenbrock, Booth, the toy multilayer regression, and teleportation; it has no license, dependency lock, tests, data, stored metrics, or code for MNIST, the schedule experiments, runtime scaling, or the Figure 8 sweep. All three supplied examples execute under a current environment and the source package compiles, but NumPy's random rotation is unseeded and teleport_SO2 updates theta after the last computed transformed point, leaving the final update unused. Executability therefore verifies only a subset of the paper and does not rescue the loss-invariance failure.

key_findings.claim: A complete equation and visual audit found two smaller source-level proof defects in addition to the substantive theorem limitations.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 36 drops the leading minus sign while transforming dL(g·w)/dt into a nonnegative squared norm; the intended invariance equality in Corollary 5.2 remains recoverable because both rates should be negative. Corollary 5.2 additionally invokes eta^(-1) after Equation 9 permits eta to be merely positive semidefinite, so its orthogonal-group definition requires the unstated stronger premise that eta is positive definite and invertible. Proposition C.2 says the solution is an eigenvector although sign and a repeated top eigenspace make it nonunique. Across all 57 numbered equations, eight figures, three algorithms, eleven distinct propositions, one corollary, one lemma, and Appendices A-D, no other comparable source-level algebraic defect was identified.

method.core_idea: Exploit an exact symmetry of the loss to relocate parameters on the same level set to a point with a larger gradient norm, then continue a conventional first-order optimizer from that point.
method.mechanism: At scheduled epochs, optimize a group element g by gradient ascent on the squared norm of the parameter gradient, transform the current parameters by g, and resume GD, SGD, or AdaGrad. Test functions pull rotations back through hand-designed invertible maps. Neural networks transform adjacent layers with GL actions; the implementation approximates the matrix exponential and inverse by I+T and I-T and uses hidden-activation pseudoinverses.
assumptions: The objective has a known differentiable invertible symmetry action that preserves the relevant loss exactly.
The orbit contains a reachable point with a larger gradient norm and the orbit optimization is stable and affordable.
The transformed optimizer state remains meaningful, especially for adaptive or stochastic methods.
The network activation is bijective and the hidden activation used in the exact GL construction is square and full rank.
Continuous gradient-flow reasoning remains informative for the chosen finite learning rate and approximate teleportation.
For the quadratic theorem, the positive-definite matrix and its induced transitive action are known and exact maximization is available.
For the Newton-direction interpretation, the level set is regular, the loss is twice differentiable, the Hessian is invertible, and the relevant Hessian eigenvalue has the required sign.

techniques.role: Move parameters between loss-equivalent representatives before resuming local optimization.
Optimize the symmetry-group element for a larger squared gradient norm.
Construct loss-invariant SO(2) actions for analytic test functions and GL actions between adjacent network layers.
Approximate a continuous GL element and its inverse by I+T and I-T for differentiable search.
Map transformed hidden activations back to weights when activation matrices are rectangular.
Relate gradient norm to instantaneous loss decay and analyze an exact quadratic special case.
Vary teleportation timing, frequency, mini-batches, ascent steps, and ascent learning rates.

evaluations.result: Figures 2 and 7 show that hand-derived SO(2) actions move GD to visually faster trajectories on both two-dimensional functions.
evaluations.baseline: Gradient descent only; the symmetry construction uses the known analytic objective and optimum.

evaluations.metric: epochs and wall time to a plateau
evaluations.result: Figure 3 reports faster GD and AdaGrad curves with teleportation over five runs, and Figure 8 reports speedup for many surviving grid-search settings.
evaluations.baseline: The same optimizer without teleportation; GD and AdaGrad use different learning rates and are not compared directly.

evaluations.metric: loss immediately before and after the released epoch-5 update
evaluations.result: Across five seeds, the released regression update changed loss by 39-91% directly, with before/after ratios 0.613, 0.132, 0.545, 0.603, and 0.090.
evaluations.baseline: Exact teleportation requires a ratio of 1 up to numerical roundoff; this implementation fails that defining invariant.

evaluations.metric: training and validation loss and training gradient norm
evaluations.result: Figures 4-5 show faster early training and stronger effects from earlier, denser, or larger-batch teleportation, but the paper reports earlier overfit, slightly worse validation accuracy, and detrimental AdaGrad validation loss.
evaluations.baseline: SGD and AdaGrad without teleportation on one shallow MLP; no test-set result or multi-seed uncertainty is given.

evaluations.metric: CPU time by matrix dimension and layer count
evaluations.result: Figure 6 is consistent with polynomial width scaling and linear layer scaling, while teleportation dominates runtime through larger constants.
evaluations.baseline: A 300-epoch GD run with ten-step teleportation every ten epochs; hardware details are absent.

evaluations.result: All eight figures were inspected: Figure 1 is conceptual, Figures 2 and 7 visualize test-function trajectories and gradients, Figures 3-5 report learning curves, Figure 6 reports scaling, and Figure 8 reports a conditional hyperparameter sweep.
evaluations.baseline: No accuracy table, statistical test, modern architecture, large-scale workload, or resource-matched second-order baseline is present.

evaluations.result: The official TeX source compiles to 20 pages in three pdfLaTeX passes, and the Rosenbrock, Booth, and regression scripts execute under current PyTorch; the fresh official PDF is byte-identical to the pinned cache.
evaluations.baseline: The code omits MNIST and three later experiment families and provides no dependency lock, tests, or stored outputs.

limitations: Instantaneous gradient-flow decay is not a discrete-iteration, wall-clock, or end-to-end convergence guarantee.
The Hazan citation omits the square on each gradient norm and does not state the associated smoothness-limited step; even the corrected aggregate bound does not imply fewer required steps.
Proposition 5.4 orders only gradient norms under a strong exponentially growing ratio, not objective values.

The positive-definite quadratic theorem depends on the known matrix A and requires the standard or another sphere-transitive representation; its stated allowance of an arbitrary representation does not imply a transitive orbit.
Proposition 5.7 omits differentiability, regular-level-set, Hessian-invertibility, and eigenvalue-sign conditions.
The practical GL orbit optimum can be unbounded or fail to exist.
The exact network action requires bijective activations and square full-rank hidden activations.
Rectangular pseudoinverses used in the reported networks do not form the claimed group action.
The first-order I+T and I-T pair is not exactly inverse and does not preserve loss in released-code checks; the code also inserts a one-half loss factor absent from the Section 6.1 objective.
Mini-batch-dependent transformations need not preserve full-dataset loss or predictions.
The test-function actions are derived from known analytic maps and optima rather than discovered.
Regression evidence is a four-example toy with hyperparameters tuned on the evaluated problem.
MNIST evidence uses one shallow MLP, omits test accuracy and error bars, and reports worse validation behavior.
No Adam, momentum, second-order optimizer, modern architecture, or large-scale task is evaluated.
Runtime results use one unspecified CPU and a plateau-based stopping rule.
Diverged and nonconverged hyperparameter settings are omitted from Figure 8.
No statistical significance or resource-matched total-compute comparison is reported.
The repository omits the MNIST, schedule, runtime, and hyperparameter-sweep experiments.
The repository has no license, pinned environment, tests, fixed NumPy seed, data, or stored metrics.

Corollary 5.2 requires invertible positive-definite eta although Equation 9 permits a positive-semidefinite matrix; Equation 36 loses a minus sign, and Proposition C.2 suppresses optimizer nonuniqueness.
failure_modes: An approximate transformation may lower the loss directly, making an apparent acceleration indistinguishable from an extra optimizer step.
A mini-batch-specific transformation can preserve or improve one batch while changing predictions and loss elsewhere.
Maximizing gradient norm without coordinating the base learning rate can produce instability or divergence.
The group-element objective may be unbounded, so gradient ascent can chase ever-larger parameter scales.
Pseudoinverse error can grow when hidden activations are rank-deficient or ill-conditioned.
Nonbijective activations such as ReLU invalidate the inverse-activation construction.
Adaptive optimizer accumulators may not transform covariantly with the teleported parameters.
A larger local gradient may point along an unfavorable or highly curved direction and need not reduce future loss faster.
Teleportation toward sharp regions can accelerate training while degrading validation performance.
A plateau stopping rule can label a stalled suboptimal run as converged.
Selecting only converged sweep settings can hide the method's sensitivity and instability.
Orbit-search and inversion overhead can outweigh any reduction in base-optimizer steps.
reusable_insights: Treat optimizer reparameterizations as interventions whose invariants must be numerically checked before interpreting learning curves.
Report loss immediately before and after every teleportation, along with full-data prediction drift and group-law residuals.
Separate exact symmetry theory from approximate implementation and bound each approximation's loss error.
Compare end-to-end wall time at a fixed target loss, including orbit search, inversions, failed searches, and hyperparameter tuning.
Transform optimizer state together with parameters or restart it explicitly and ablate that choice.
Use a constrained or projected level-set operator when the symmetry-orbit maximization is unbounded.
Distinguish a hand-constructed symmetry oracle from a method that discovers useful symmetries in realistic models.
Evaluate whether steeper representatives improve generalization as well as training speed, because sharpness can reverse the benefit.
Require modern architectures, multiple datasets, multiple seeds, test metrics, and strong tuned optimizers before claiming practical acceleration.
open_questions: Can a scalable transformation provably keep full-dataset loss invariant for nonbijective modern networks without layerwise pseudoinverses?
What convergence rate follows when the teleportation operator is approximate, nontransitive, expensive, and invoked only intermittently?
How should momentum, Adam moments, weight decay, normalization state, and distributed optimizer state transform under a symmetry?
Can orbit search be regularized so that a finite maximizer exists without erasing the gradient-norm benefit?
Which invariant objective predicts useful future progress better than raw gradient norm under a finite learning rate?
Does teleportation improve time to a held-out metric after matching total FLOPs, wall time, tuning budget, and instability rate?
Can useful parameter symmetries be discovered from a model and data rather than analytically supplied?
How much of Figure 3 remains after replacing the released approximate update with an exactly loss-preserving transformation?
When does moving to sharper representatives harm calibration or generalization even if training loss falls faster?

competitive_landscape.title: Symmetry-invariant optimization in deep networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct prior use of parameter-space symmetry to redesign neural-network optimization.
competitive_landscape.difference: Badrinarayanan et al. quotient out scaling reparameterizations with symmetry-invariant gradient updates instead of moving deliberately along an invariant orbit to maximize gradient norm. It predates the reviewed paper's broad claim that symmetry can accelerate optimization and provides MNIST plus segmentation evidence with cheap updates.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Teleportation
competitive_landscape.relationship: The closest direct predecessor: function-preserving movement in neural-network weight space with altered gradients and loss geometry.
competitive_landscape.difference: Armenta et al. establish the teleportation concept, explore level curves, and report random teleportation and gradient boosting. The reviewed paper's main increment is to optimize the teleportation destination for gradient norm, generalize the group-action framing, and attempt rate analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Improving Convergence and Generalization Using Parameter Symmetries
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct same-author successor extending teleportation theory, optimizer coverage, meta-learning, and generalization analysis.
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhao et al. explicitly target overall time to convergence rather than the reviewed paper's instantaneous and finite-gradient comparisons, and study curvature-selected minima and a wider range of optimizers. Its existence also confirms that the reviewed paper did not settle the mechanism or end-to-end rate question.

competitive_landscape.title: Level Set Teleportation: An Optimization Perspective
competitive_landscape.relationship: The strongest current direct theoretical competitor for maximizing gradient norm over an objective level set.
competitive_landscape.difference: Mishkin et al. state that prior work lacked convex convergence theory, guarantees for solving the teleportation operator, and clear acceleration evidence. They prove a conditional faster rate under Hessian stability, show no improvement in the standard strongly convex setting, and implement projected level-set search with Hessian-vector products, directly narrowing and repairing the reviewed paper's broad acceleration interpretation.

competitive_landscape.title: Teleportation With Null Space Gradient Projection for Optimization Acceleration
competitive_landscape.relationship: A current direct implementation competitor aimed at preserving the loss level set while scaling beyond MLPs.
competitive_landscape.difference: Wu et al. project the teleportation objective gradient into an input null space and target CNNs and transformers. Their motivation explicitly identifies prior teleportation as expensive and largely restricted to MLPs, the same practical weaknesses exposed by this paper's pseudoinverse construction and incomplete artifact.

competitive_landscape.title: Continual Optimization with Symmetry Teleportation for Multi-Task Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: A current application-specific competitor replacing explicit group actions with low-rank adaptations and loss-invariance objectives.
competitive_landscape.difference: COST triggers teleportation on multi-task gradient conflict, uses LoRA instead of the reviewed paper's bijective-activation pseudoinverse action, and reuses optimizer trajectories. Its limitations discussion explicitly says earlier schemes are impractical for modern deep models because of bijectivity and pseudoinverse requirements.

competitive_landscape.title: Improving Learning to Optimize Using Parameter Symmetries
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct learning-to-optimize successor that learns symmetry transformations and local updates rather than solving every orbit search online.
competitive_landscape.difference: Zamir et al. add a benchmark, momentum, and conditions under which a meta-optimizer can learn a useful transformation, but also report that vanilla learning-to-optimize consistently beats the teleportation-augmented variant on both tested function families. This supplies direct negative evidence against treating teleportation as a generally beneficial add-on.

competitive_landscape.title: The Role of Symmetry in Optimizing Overparameterized Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: A current symmetry-based account of how overparameterization changes optimization geometry and access to equivalent solutions.
competitive_landscape.difference: Sareen et al. analyze symmetry as diagonal Hessian preconditioning and increased probability mass near global minima, with width-controlled teacher-student evidence. This offers a conditioning and reachability mechanism rather than the reviewed paper's gradient-norm-maximizing jumps and tests it across width growth.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim an accelerated gradient-based optimizer that exploits loss-landscape symmetries, derives group actions for test functions and multilayer networks, characterizes when teleportation improves current and subsequent steps, relates optimal teleportation to Newton's method, and speeds GD and AdaGrad empirically.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper does formulate gradient-norm orbit search clearly, constructs analytic and neural actions, supplies an instantaneous chain-rule result, a finite gradient-norm persistence condition, an exact positive-quadratic example, and experiments spanning two test functions, toy regression, and MNIST.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Novelty is moderate and historically meaningful rather than foundationally complete. Neural Teleportation already supplied function-preserving relocation and gradient boosting, while earlier symmetry-aware optimizers already used parameter invariance. The new purposeful search for a steep orbit representative is a real contribution, but its broad acceleration narrative outruns the theory, and its central neural evidence is confounded because the released approximate update changes loss directly. Later work supplies the missing convergence qualifications and more scalable operators; a direct learning-to-optimize successor also reports settings where adding teleportation consistently underperforms its vanilla optimizer.

verification.passage_check: Independently re-read all 20 physical pages of the exact pinned arXiv v3 PDF and checked every existing finding and page anchor against the source, including all 57 numbered equations, eight figures, three algorithms, eleven distinct propositions, one corollary, one lemma, and Appendices A-D. Re-derived the quadratic orbit argument and Corollary 5.2 premises, checked the Hazan citation, visually inspected every figure page, and independently reproduced the five released regression teleportations and their gradient-norm changes. The secondary pass added the omitted squared-norm citation error, eta invertibility premise, representation-transitivity restriction, and paper/code half-loss mismatch; all other claims and anchors were confirmed.
verification.competitor_check: Independently rechecked the six recorded direct primary papers at their exact current arXiv or official-proceedings revisions and searched successor, implementation, theory, and negative-result query families through 2026-08-24. Added arXiv:2504.15399v1, a direct learning-to-optimize successor with negative teleportation results on both tested function families, and arXiv:2604.25150v3, a current symmetry-as-conditioning and reachability account. The resulting eight-paper panel covers the direct precursor, foundational symmetry-aware optimizer, same-author extension, level-set theory, scalable null-space implementation, multi-task application, learned teleportation boundary, and current overparameterization mechanism.

reviewer_notes: Exact-source audit used the pinned 20-page arXiv v3 PDF; local PDF and text hashes match the full-text index, and a fresh official PDF downloaded on 2026-08-24 was byte-identical. The exact unversioned source locator remains https://export.arxiv.org/pdf/2205.10637. The official record remains v3, revised 2023-01-04, and the NeurIPS proceedings list the paper in the 2022 main track. Every page was rendered and inspected, covering all eight figures, no tables, three algorithms, 57 numbered equations, one assumption, eleven distinct propositions including appendix results, one corollary, one lemma, Appendices A-D, and all 29 rendered references. The official e-print package (SHA-256 80d8ed1b81b8450d075bd7b52e438c953ce1016d4ea122fa24fa9c20d5e01b5a) contains 55 files including TeX and 40 figure PDFs; it compiled successfully in three pdfLaTeX passes to 20 pages under a current TeX environment. The first-party repository https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/Symmetry-Teleportation was audited at commit db1981477baa8e8cd68879348a39a0494e46628b (latest commit 2022-11-09). Its three examples compiled and ran under Python with PyTorch 2.12.0, Matplotlib 3.5.2, and NumPy 1.26.4, but the repository is a partial, unpinned artifact with no license or tests and omits MNIST, schedule, scaling, and sweep code. Direct execution of the paper-specified regression teleport found large loss changes across five seeds, contradicting the loss-invariant premise; the independent secondary pass reproduced the five loss jumps and gradient-squared ratios. Eight direct competitors were revision-checked against primary arXiv or official proceedings records through 2026-08-24. Promotion to verified records the independent review by reviewer-f1b20ae52195 while preserving the original source hashes and locator.
